title: sandhi plainly
hook: a group chat called family, and an old line with a join inside it: vasudhaiva kutumbakam
tomorrow: why would anyone chant a verse with every word pulled apart?

segments.voice: Yesterday, sandhi plainly: a t that gets ready for its neighbor, and the world still inside Jagannath. Today, a join that holds the whole earth.

A group chat named family usually has a handful of people in it. Maybe a cousin's husband got added once and never left. Who belongs in it is a question much older than phones. An old Sanskrit line answers it in two words, and the first one hides a join: vasudhaiva kutumbakam. The whole earth is family.
screen: `A GROUP CHAT CALLED FAMILY.` → `WHO BELONGS IN IT?` → `VASUDHAIVA KUTUMBAKAM.`

segments.voice: Undo the join first. Vasudha is the earth. Eva means indeed. When a long a meets an e, they don't sit side by side; they fold into ai. Vasudhaiva: the earth, indeed. Kutumbakam: a household, a family. The line comes from the Maha Upanishad, and a version of it sits in the Hitopadesha, a book of fables. The full verse is sharper than the slogan. This one is mine, that one's a stranger: that's how the narrow-hearted count. For those whose ways are generous, the whole earth is family. It isn't saying everyone is the same. It's saying who you count as yours depends on how wide your heart is. A neighbor tradition says something close, in its own words. In the Bible, the apostle Paul tells the people of Athens that God "hath made of one blood all nations of men for to dwell on all the face of the earth." Both lines refuse to stop the family at the edge of a tribe. The honest difference: Paul starts from where people come from, one blood, one maker. The Sanskrit verse starts from the one doing the counting, and how wide that person's heart is. One looks back to an origin. The other looks out from the heart. Neither line says who will be at the table tonight. That's left to the one who reads it.
screen: `VASUDHA + EVA = VASUDHAIVA.` · `NARROW HEARTS COUNT MINE AND STRANGER.` · `ACTS: ONE BLOOD, ALL NATIONS.` · `ONE ORIGIN. ONE WIDE HEART.` · then, large: `THE WHOLE EARTH IS FAMILY.`

segments.voice: Count on your fingers the people who treated you like family without having to: a neighbor, a teacher, a friend's parent, a stranger on a hard day. For each one, one slow breath, and a quiet thank-you.
Sandhi plainly: today, a long a and an e folding into ai, in vasudhaiva, the earth indeed.
Something to keep: sandhi plainly joins two words, and the verse joins the whole earth into one family. Until tomorrow.

howItsDone: Vasudhaiva kutumbakam is quoted by Hindus at weddings, in speeches and on public buildings in India, usually in its short form; the full verse contrasts the narrow-hearted and the generous.

fork.setup: your cousin says vasudhaiva kutumbakam means every religion teaches the same thing. what's a fairer reading of the verse?
options: it's about who you count as yours: generous hearts count the whole earth.
he's right: the line teaches that all religions are identical.
it's only about blood relatives, the household at home.
fork.reveal: the full verse sets the narrow-hearted, who count 'mine' and 'stranger', against the generous, for whom the earth is family. it widens the family without erasing differences.

original.note: Sanskrit: vasudhaiva kuṭumbakam, the earth indeed is family; vasudhā + eva, joined.

trapdoor: what you thought: vasudhaiva is one long word.
what it means: vasudha, the earth, plus eva, indeed, folded into ai: the earth indeed is family.
what a scholar hears: vriddhi sandhi, a or ā before e giving ai (Ashtadhyayi 6.1.88); and a verse that sets the narrow-hearted's counting against the generous.
recall: jagat, the world, plus natha, lord

chat.says: the girl after me reads a Bible line: 'made of one blood all nations.' are our lines the same?
options: close kin: both widen the family. hers starts from one blood, yours from a wide heart.
yes, identical: both lines mean exactly the same thing, in two languages.
not really: hers is about God, and yours is only a saying about manners.
chat.meaning: Both refuse to stop the family at a tribe's edge. Acts begins from one blood and one maker; the Sanskrit verse from how wide the heart counts.

notes: 2026-10-14 v3 rewrite (recipe v3, shape wisdom; the weekly unity thread): new lesson recipe data (chat, gloss, recall) included; confirm the chat reply, glosses, scripts and pronunciations with the Keeper.

This day's angle changed in v3: the earlier draft taught an r that reaches ahead and curls an n (Ramayana, Narayana; Ashtadhyayi 8.4.1-3; Manusmriti 1.10). The wisdom shape and the owner's unity thread ('more alike than we think', one human race) called for one question, the tradition's answer, and one neighbor tradition, so the day now teaches vriddhi sandhi (a/ā + e = ai, 6.1.88) through vasudhaiva kutumbakam. Title, word and carry kept. The ṇ-after-r rule could return on a later sandhi day.

Unity thread: shared with Christianity (Acts 17:26, KJV, quoted exactly) that the human family doesn't stop at a tribe's edge. Honest difference: Acts grounds it in one origin (one blood, one maker); the Sanskrit verse in the width of the counter's heart. Ranks neither; the myth and fork explicitly say the line doesn't mean 'all religions are the same'.

Confirm the verse reference (Maha Upanishad 6.71-72; some editions number it 6.71 or 6.72) and the Hitopadesha location (Mitralabha, the jackal and the deer story). The paraphrase 'narrow-hearted' renders laghucetasām; the Hitopadesha's first line reads ayaṃ nijaḥ paro veti. 'A later Upanishad' in the gloss: confirm wording.
howItsDone says the line appears 'on public buildings in India': it is inscribed in the entrance hall of India's Parliament House; soften to 'in speeches and at weddings' if the Keeper prefers.
Priya storyline: at the send-off, the classmate reading after her has Acts 17:26; Priya notices what's shared and what's different. No religion is assigned to Sam.
